evals.prompt: We need to add scheduled invoice reminders to our SaaS app. This will touch the billing service, email delivery, user notification preferences, and a new retry policy for failed sends. Can you implement it?
evals.expected_output: The agent should NOT start implementation. It should run the five-gate design process, clarify the problem and constraints, and produce a design brief for approval before any code is written.
assertions: The agent does NOT start writing implementation code immediately
The agent frames the problem before discussing implementation details
The agent asks or states relevant constraints such as delivery timing, retries, user preferences, and failure handling
The agent identifies that the feature is non-trivial because it spans multiple files or concerns
The agent produces or promises a design brief before implementation

evals.prompt: /design We want to add organization-level SSO to our product. This will affect login flow, user provisioning, account linking, and admin settings. Please think it through first.
evals.expected_output: The agent should explicitly run the full design flow, covering problem framing, context, options, architecture, and routing, then end with a structured design brief instead of code.
assertions: The response covers problem framing rather than jumping straight to SAML or OIDC implementation details
The response includes context analysis such as current auth flow, provisioning behavior, and deployment constraints
The response evaluates at least two distinct approaches or integration options
The response includes an architecture sketch with boundaries, data flow, or failure modes
The response includes an ordered skill-routing or implementation sequence
The response ends with a design brief or approval checkpoint before implementation

evals.prompt: Review this design for a new Redis cache layer in our checkout service. The proposal says: 'Add Redis in front of every database call so checkout is faster. Engineering will figure out invalidation during implementation.'
evals.expected_output: The agent should switch to review mode, evaluate the proposal against the gates, and flag what is missing instead of accepting the design at face value.
assertions: The agent identifies missing problem framing such as unclear targets or unclear user-facing outcome
The agent flags missing context analysis such as current bottlenecks or existing data flow
The agent notes that solution evaluation is incomplete because only one approach is presented
The agent flags architecture risk around cache invalidation, coupling, or failure modes
The agent does NOT approve the design as sufficient without additional gate evidence

evals.prompt: What's the scope of adding audit logs for admin actions across our API, background jobs, and internal dashboard? I need to know what to investigate first.
evals.expected_output: The agent should run in scope mode and return a prioritized checklist, highlighting the gates that deserve the most attention rather than producing a full implementation plan.
assertions: The response is framed as scope analysis or a prioritized checklist
The response identifies cross-cutting concerns such as API paths, async jobs, retention, and who consumes the logs
The response highlights which gates need the most attention, such as context and architecture
The agent does NOT jump into code or detailed implementation steps

evals.prompt: Should we build our new multi-tenant reporting feature by adding tenant_id everywhere in the current service, or by extracting a separate reporting pipeline and store?
evals.expected_output: The agent should evaluate multiple approaches using trade-offs and ideality, not anchor on the first option or choose based on novelty alone.
assertions: The agent compares at least two distinct approaches
The agent discusses benefits, resource costs, and harmful effects or operational burden
The agent treats hidden coupling or maintenance cost as part of the decision
The agent chooses an approach with explicit rationale instead of saying 'it depends' without analysis

evals.prompt: How do I parse JSON into a struct in Go?
evals.expected_output: The agent should recognize this as a single implementation question and avoid forcing the full five-gate design workflow.
assertions: The agent does NOT run the full design-thinking process for this simple question
The agent does NOT produce a five-gate design brief
The agent answers directly or routes to a more appropriate implementation skill

evals.name: scoped-architecture-discovery-handoff
evals.prompt: Before choosing a design, we need evidence about ownership drift and candidate boundaries across catalog, benefit, and authentication. The product outcome is framed, but the current architecture is not yet mapped.
evals.expected_output: Pause design context analysis and hand a bounded evidence-gathering scope to architecture review, with an explicit return condition before option selection.
assertions: The agent does not invent architecture evidence
The agent names improve-codebase-architecture as the next owner
The handoff includes scope, constraints, evidence questions, and return condition
The agent pauses design until scoped discovery returns

evals.name: accepted-behavior-handoff
evals.prompt: The design brief is approved for an authenticated catalog endpoint in Go. Public behavior, response envelope, pagination, errors, boundaries, risks, and implementation scope are all settled. Implement it test-first.
evals.expected_output: Hand the accepted brief directly to TDD as implementation owner without requesting the same approval again.
assertions: The agent names tdd-go as the next owner
The handoff includes accepted behavior, interface, scope, risks, and evidence
The agent does not ask for duplicate design approval
The agent does not route an approved new behavior to cleanup

evals.name: accepted-cleanup-handoff
evals.prompt: The approved end state removes one internal adapter and its dead aliases. Public behavior remains unchanged, compatibility evidence is complete, and deletion scope and rollback are settled.
evals.expected_output: Hand the accepted end state, invariants, and compatibility ledger directly to bounded cleanup without starting a new behavior cycle.
assertions: The agent names zero-tech-debt as the next owner
The handoff includes end state, scope, invariants, authority, and compatibility evidence
The agent does not invoke TDD for unchanged behavior
The agent does not rerun architecture discovery for an accepted candidate

evals.name: linked-skills-are-not-mandatory-pipeline
evals.prompt: These four skills are linked. For an approved pure cleanup that preserves behavior, should every linked skill run automatically before work begins?
evals.expected_output: Explain that links are conditional routes, select cleanup directly, and name the concrete triggers that would justify another owner.
assertions: The agent does NOT invoke all four skills merely because they are linked
The agent routes directly to zero-tech-debt for the accepted structural cleanup
The agent preserves existing behavior tests rather than starting a new TDD behavior cycle
The agent names the trigger that would justify routing back to design, review, or TDD

evals.name: public-api-composes-contract-and-tdd
evals.prompt: Design a new public REST endpoint in the Go backend service, reconcile it with related PHP behavior, then implement it after the contract is approved.
evals.expected_output: Compose API-contract design inside the design phase, return for acceptance, and route accepted behavior to TDD; backend-go-testing supplies mechanics inside that owner.
assertions: The sequence includes engineering-rest-api-design before contract acceptance
The contract returns to engineering-design-thinking for the decision
Accepted behavior routes to tdd-go
backend-go-testing does not replace tdd-go as phase owner

evals.name: solution-smuggled-problem-frame
evals.prompt: Add Kafka so profile updates appear instantly. We saw one 700 ms dashboard trace and support expects under 300 ms, but no latency breakdown exists.
evals.expected_output: Challenge the proposed mechanism and create a solution-free Problem Frame before comparing implementations.
assertions: Separates the proposed Kafka solution from the user-visible problem
Names stakeholders, actual state and evidence, expected state, and the gap
Labels constraints, assumptions, cause hypotheses, and abstraction level
Defines success evidence without inventing a baseline

evals.name: first-principles-mode
evals.prompt: Our familiar caching pattern conflicts with the consistency requirement in this unfamiliar offline-sync architecture. Derive the decision instead of copying the usual pattern.
evals.expected_output: Use first-principles mode to separate evidence from convention and rebuild options from fundamentals with a bounded stopping rule.
assertions: Separates verified facts, conventions, and assumptions
Decomposes one causal layer deeper into fundamentals and interactions
Derives options rather than treating a known pattern as proof
Uses a timebox or evidence threshold to prevent analysis paralysis

evals.name: contradiction-before-compromise
evals.prompt: We need strict global ordering and maximum write throughput. Pick a reasonable compromise and move on.
evals.expected_output: Test whether the apparent trade-off is a removable contradiction before accepting a compromise.
assertions: States both desired properties and the condition creating conflict
Tests separation in time, space, condition, and parts versus whole
Compares any remaining compromise using benefits, resources, and harmful effects
Does not promise impossible properties or accept compromise by default

evals.name: expectation-is-part-of-gap
evals.prompt: Users expect a live answer for a report that requires a two-hour external data refresh. The current system returns the correct report after the refresh. Frame the problem.
evals.expected_output: Treat the problem as an actual-versus-expected gap and consider changing the expectation as well as changing the system.
assertions: Identifies the stakeholder and the actual-versus-expected gap
Separates the underlying job from the demand for a live answer
Considers expectation design as a legitimate option
Defines evidence that would show whether the gap is closed

evals.name: close-learning-loop
evals.prompt: The design was implemented and shipped. The chosen queue reduced median latency but doubled timeout errors. Update the decision model.
evals.expected_output: Connect the original claim and evidence to the decision, observed outcome, and an explicit model update.
assertions: Records the original claim and supporting evidence
Compares the observed outcome with the success evidence
Updates or reverses the decision rather than defending it
Captures a reusable model update with scope and limits

evals.name: typescript-backend-complexity
evals.prompt: Design a TypeScript order backend that applies pricing rules, writes Postgres, calls a payment gateway, and publishes an event. The team is split between one large OrderService class and rewriting everything as pure functions.
evals.expected_output: Classify the complexity and combine explicit functional data flow with role-first object isolation only where state, effects, lifecycle, or adapters require it.
assertions: Distinguishes essential domain rules from accidental design complexity
Scans the relevant mutable-state, side-effect, dependency, control-flow, and code-size axes
States which complexity is reduced, isolated, or accepted
Designs messages, roles, and contracts before TypeScript classes
Uses composition rather than inheritance and rejects both the god class and forced all-functions rewrite
Separates direct core tests from process-boundary integration evidence

evals.name: simple-crud-counterexample
evals.prompt: A local admin-only CRUD path has one handler, one database operation, no domain rules, no external integration, and no expected variants. Should we introduce Functional Core / Imperative Shell and repository interfaces?
evals.expected_output: Keep the direct local flow unless evidence shows a real moving part or seam; do not create ceremonial architecture.
assertions: Does not impose Functional Core / Imperative Shell
Does not create an interface for one adapter without a real variation
Explains that extra layers would relocate or add complexity rather than reduce it
Recommends verification proportional to the simple database contract

evals.name: non-go-implementation-handoff
evals.prompt: The accepted implementation is a TypeScript backend change. Behavior, public contract, scope, and risks are settled. Which owner should receive the implementation handoff?
evals.expected_output: Use the target repository's concrete TypeScript test-first workflow, preserving the standard handoff artifact, without routing the code to the Go-only TDD skill.
assertions: Does not route TypeScript implementation to tdd-go
Names the target project's test-first workflow or repository conventions
Carries accepted behavior, interface, scope, risks, and verification state
Does not request duplicate design approval

evals.name: go-backend-complexity
evals.prompt: Design a Go order backend that applies pricing rules, writes Postgres, calls a payment gateway, and publishes an event. The team proposes either a Java-style interface for every struct or one large service struct.
evals.expected_output: Use functions and values to reduce avoidable moving parts, structs and small consumer-owned interfaces to isolate necessary state and effects, and no class-emulation ceremony.
assertions: Distinguishes essential domain rules from accidental design complexity and scans the five axes
States which complexity is reduced, isolated, or accepted
Uses functions and values for deterministic rules where they remove mutation or temporal coupling
Uses structs for cohesive state or dependencies and small consumer-owned interfaces only at real seams
States that an imperative shell does not require classes and rejects interface-per-struct ceremony
Separates pure core tests from adapter integration or contract tests and critical end-to-end evidence

evals.name: go-package-cycle-philosophy
evals.prompt: A Go backend has orders importing inventory to reserve stock, while inventory imports orders to read order state. The team proposes adding common, plus global handlers, services, repositories, and models packages. Redesign the package graph.
evals.expected_output: Preserve business-capability locality and a dependency DAG; resolve the cycle through ownership, merge, or a consumer-owned contract rather than technical-layer packages or a common dumping ground.
assertions: Defaults to business-capability locality and fewer packages instead of global technical-layer buckets
Keeps names contextual and types near their owning transport, persistence, or domain boundary
Requires a directed acyclic dependency graph and identifies Go as compile-time enforcement
Tries moving responsibility or merging a fake boundary before introducing an interface
Places any necessary interface at the consumer and rejects common as a vague dumping ground

evals.name: typescript-cycle-is-stack-neutral
evals.prompt: A TypeScript backend has billing importing notifications to send receipts, while notifications imports billing to format invoice data. It builds today. Should we ignore the circular import or create a shared service layer?
evals.expected_output: Apply the stack-neutral ownership and DAG principle even though TypeScript may permit the import cycle, without manufacturing a generic shared service layer.
assertions: Does not ignore the cycle merely because the project builds
Explains the ownership, hidden-coupling, initialization, or independent-change risk
Rejects a generic shared layer unless it is a real owned concept
Uses a small consumer-owned contract only if billing and notifications remain independently owned
Treats Go as a stronger enforcement example rather than the owner of the design principle
